claim: Ground self-righting is a critical locomotor capability that animals must have to survive.
source: Ground self-righting is a critical locomotor capability that animals must have to survive (for a review, see Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article (Li et al., 2019)

claim: The longer an animal is flipped over and stranded, the more susceptible it is to risks like predation, starvation, desiccation, and limited mating success.
source: The longer an animal is flipped over and stranded, the more susceptible it is to risks like predation, starvation, desiccation (Steyermark and Spotila, 2001), and limited mating success (Penn and Jane Brockmann, 1995).

claim: Ground self-righting is critical for the continuous operation of mobile robots.

claim: To self-right, cockroaches must overcome potential energy barriers seven times greater than the mechanical energy required per stride for steady-state, medium speed running (eight body lengths s−1).
source: For example, to self-right, cockroaches must overcome potential energy barriers seven times greater than the mechanical energy required per stride for steady-state, medium speed running (eight body lengths s−1) (Kram et al., 1997)

claim: Cockroaches must exert ground reaction forces eight times greater than that during steady-state medium speed running (five body lengths s−1) to self-right.

claim: Ground self-righting has been studied in a diversity of animals, including insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and vertebrates.

claim: Animals use appendages such as legs, wings, tail, and neck together with body deformation to propel and perturb the body to destabilize from the upside-down state.

source: This finding suggested that potential energy landscape modeling can be used to understand stereotyped ground self-righting strategies of other species (Ashe, 1970; Domokos and Várkonyi, 2008; Golubović et al., 2013; Li et al., 2019; O'Donnel, 2018)
evidence: Suggestion based on findings, with citations to studies of other species

claim: Potential energy landscape modeling can be used to infer self-righting strategies of extinct species.
source: and even infer those of extinct species (analogous to Gatesy et al., 2009).
evidence: Suggestion based on findings, with analogy to Gatesy et al., 2009

claim: Potential energy landscape modeling will inform the design and control of self-righting robots.
source: Similarly, it will inform the design and control of self-righting robots (e.g., Caporale et al., 2020; Kessens et al., 2012).
evidence: Suggestion based on findings, with citations to robot studies

claim: The potential energy landscape approach can in principle be applied to more complex and different self-righting behaviors, as well as on ground of different properties.
source: Although only demonstrated in a model system, the potential energy landscape approach can in principle be applied to more complex and different self-righting behaviors, as well as on ground of different properties (Sasaki and Nonaka, 2016), to understand how propelling and perturbing effects work together.
evidence: Suggestion based on findings, with citation to Sasaki and Nonaka, 2016

claim: As the ground becomes more rugged with larger asperities, the landscape becomes more rugged with more attractive basins.
source: For example, as the ground becomes more rugged with larger asperities, the landscape becomes more rugged with more attractive basins (Figure 8, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Example shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—video 1

claim: The potential energy landscape approach does not apply to highly dynamic self-righting strategies, such as those using jumping where kinetic energy far exceeds the potential energy barrier.
source: However, this approach does not apply to highly dynamic self-righting strategies, such as those using jumping (Bolmin et al., 2017; Kovac et al., 2008) where kinetic energy far exceeds the potential energy barrier.
evidence: Limitation of the approach, with citations to jumping strategies

claim: The potential energy landscape model does not describe self-righting dynamics.
source: The potential energy landscape model here does not describe self-righting dynamics.
evidence: Limitation of the model described in the manuscript

claim: Recent dynamic modeling using multi-body dynamics simulations revealed that wing-leg coordination affects self-righting by changing the mechanical energy budget.
source: Recent dynamic modeling using multi-body dynamics simulations (Xuan and Li, 2020a) and dynamical templates (Xuan and Li, 2020b) in our lab revealed that wing-leg coordination affects self-righting by changing the mechanical energy budget (Xuan and Li, 2020b)
evidence: Supported by citations to Xuan and Li, 2020a and 2020b

claim: The randomness in the animal's motion helps it self-right.
source: and that the randomness in the animal's motion helps it self-right (Xuan and Li, 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xuan and Li, 2020a

claim: Multi-body dynamic simulations are effectively experiments on a computer.
source: However, these approaches have their limitations: multi-body dynamic simulations are effectively experiments on a computer;
evidence: Characterization of simulation approach

claim: Dynamical templates are increasingly challenging to develop as system degrees of freedom increases.
source: dynamical templates are increasingly challenging to develop as system degrees of freedom increases.
evidence: Limitation of dynamical template approach

claim: A potential energy landscape theory that adds stochastic, non-conservative forces may be a relatively simple yet intuitive way to model probabilistic barrier-crossing dynamics.
source: Further development of a potential energy landscape theory that adds stochastic, non-conservative forces to predict how the system 'diffuses' across landscape barriers (analogous to Socci et al., 1996) may be a relatively simple yet intuitive way to model probabilistic barrier-crossing dynamics.
evidence: Suggestion for future work, with analogy to Socci et al., 1996

claim: Adult male Blaberus discoidalis cockroaches were used in the study.
source: We used 30 adult male Blaberus discoidalis cockroaches (Figure 2A) (Pinellas County Reptiles, St. Petersburg, FL), as females were often gravid and under different load-bearing conditions.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

claim: Females were not used because they were often gravid and under different load-bearing conditions.
source: We used 30 adult male Blaberus discoidalis cockroaches (Figure 2A) (Pinellas County Reptiles, St. Petersburg, FL), as females were often gravid and under different load-bearing conditions.
evidence: Justification for experimental design

claim: Animals weighed 2.6 ± 0.2 g and measured 5.3 ± 0.2 cm in length, 2.3 ± 0.1 cm in width, and 0.8 ± 0.1 cm in thickness.
source: Animals weighed 2.6 ± 0.2 g and measured 5.3 ± 0.2 cm in length, 2.3 ± 0.1 cm in width, and 0.8 ± 0.1 cm in thickness.
evidence: Measurement of animal physical characteristics

claim: Stainless steel spheres of diameter 0.32 cm and mass 0.14 g (5% of body weight, 180% of leg weight) were attached to the tibia-tarsus joint of both hind legs for leg modification.
source: We attached stainless steel spheres of diameter 0.32 cm and mass 0.14 g (5% of body weight, 180% of leg weight; Kram et al., 1997) (McMaster-Carr, Elmhurst, IL) to the tibia-tarsus joint of both hind legs (Figure 2A, Figure 3—video 1, right) using ultraviolet curing glue (BONDIC, Ontario, Canada).
evidence: Description of experimental manipulation

claim: The added mass increased the average kinetic energy during leg flailing.
source: We verified that the added mass increased the average kinetic energy during leg flailing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, see section 'Kinetic energy measurement').
evidence: Verification of experimental manipulation effect

claim: A flat, wooden surface (60 cm × 60 cm) covered with cardstock and walled with transparent acrylic sheets was used as the righting arena.
source: We used a flat, wooden surface (60 cm × 60 cm) covered with cardstock and walled with transparent acrylic sheets as the righting arena.
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: The arena was maintained at an ambient temperature of 40 ± 2°C during experiment.
source: We maintained the arena at an ambient temperature of 40 ± 2°C during experiment.
evidence: Description of experimental conditions

claim: Two synchronized cameras were used at 200 frames s−1 and 200 µs shutter time to record the self-righting maneuver from top and side views.
source: We used two synchronized cameras (Fastec IL5, Fastec Imaging, San Diego, CA) at 200 frames s−1 and 200 µs shutter time to record the self-righting maneuver from top (1200 × 1080 pixels) and side (1200 × 400 pixels) views, with a small lens aperture to maximize the focal depth of field.
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: Each animal was allowed to rest for approximately 30 minutes before its next trial to minimize the effects of fatigue.
source: After each trial, we returned the animal to its container and continued testing a different animal. This way, each animal was allowed to rest for ≈ 30 min before its next trial to minimize the effects of fatigue (Camhi, 1977).
evidence: Description of experimental protocol, with citation to Camhi, 1977

claim: 30 animals were tested, each with five trials with its hind legs intact and then modified, resulting in a total of 300 accepted trials.
source: We tested 30 animals, each with five trials with its hind legs intact and then modified, resulting in a total of 300 accepted trials (N = 30 animals, n = 150 trials for each leg treatment).
evidence: Description of experimental design and sample size

claim: Trials in which the animal collided with the walls of the righting arena or moved out of both camera views were excluded.
source: We excluded trials in which the animal collided with the walls of the righting arena or moved out of both camera views.
evidence: Description of data exclusion criteria

claim: The animal did not always immediately begin to self-right when placed on the arena.
source: Because the animal did not always immediately begin to self-right when placed on the arena (Camhi, 1977; Li et al., 2019), we defined the beginning of the self-righting attempt as the instant when the animal began moving its body or appendages to self-right.
evidence: Observation supported by citations to Camhi, 1977 and Li et al., 2019

claim: The animal was defined to have successfully self-righted if it attained an upright orientation with all six legs on the ground within 10 s of starting its attempt.
source: We defined the animal to have successfully self-righted if it attained an upright orientation with all six legs on the ground within 10 s of starting its attempt.
evidence: Definition of success criterion

claim: DeepLabCut was used to track the tip and femur-tibia joint of both hind legs, head anterior tip, abdomen posterior tip, and body midpoint.
source: We used DeepLabCut (Mathis et al., 2018) to track the tip and femur-tibia joint of both hind legs, head anterior tip, abdomen posterior tip, and body midpoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Description of tracking method, with citation to Mathis et al., 2018

claim: Direct Linear Transformation software DLTdv5 was used to reconstruct 3D motion of the tracked points.
source: We then used Direct Linear Transformation software DLTdv5 (Hedrick, 2008) to reconstruct 3D motion of the tracked points and used a sixth-order Butterworth filter with a cut-off frequency of 25 Hz to filter their 3D positions.
evidence: Description of 3D reconstruction method, with citation to Hedrick, 2008

claim: The animal body was approximated as an ellipsoid cut into two parts at 38% of total length from the anterior end, connected by a hinge joint.
source: To calculate kinetic energy, we approximated the animal body as an ellipsoid cut into two parts at 38% of total length from the anterior end, connected by a hinge joint (thorax-abdomen joint, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Description of modeling approximation

claim: Uniform mass distribution was assumed for both body parts.
source: We assumed uniform mass distribution for both parts.
evidence: Description of modeling assumption

claim: The geometric center of the body parts when their fore-aft axes are aligned was used to approximate body center of mass.
source: We used the geometric center of the body parts when their fore-aft axes are aligned to approximate body center of mass (Kram et al., 1997).
evidence: Description of modeling approximation, with citation to Kram et al., 1997

claim: Wing opening and leg flailing did not show temporal correlation.
source: In addition, wing opening and leg flailing did not show temporal correlation.
evidence: Analysis result described in the manuscript

claim: The approximate time period of leg flailing (100 ms) was comparable to combined sensory feedback (6–40 ms) and neuromuscular (45 ms) delays.
source: Furthermore, the approximate time period of leg flailing (100 ms) was comparable to combined sensory feedback (6–40 ms; Ritzmann et al., 2012) and neuromuscular (45 ms; Sponberg and Full, 2008) delays.
evidence: Comparison with values from literature, with citations to Ritzmann et al., 2012 and Sponberg and Full, 2008

claim: Previous studies observed minimal proprioceptive sensory input from legs during flailing.
source: These, combined with the fact that previous studies observed minimal proprioceptive sensory input from legs during flailing (Camhi, 1977; Delcomyn, 1987; Zill, 1986), indicate that leg flailing was more feedforward-driven than a feedback-controlled reflex coordinated with wing opening (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Camhi, 1977; Delcomyn, 1987; Zill, 1986

claim: Leg flailing was more feedforward-driven than a feedback-controlled reflex coordinated with wing opening.
source: These, combined with the fact that previous studies observed minimal proprioceptive sensory input from legs during flailing (Camhi, 1977; Delcomyn, 1987; Zill, 1986), indicate that leg flailing was more feedforward-driven than a feedback-controlled reflex coordinated with wing opening (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence

claim: Large trial-to-trial variations in the number of attempts required to self-right showed that the animal's self-righting was stochastic.
source: Moreover, large trial-to-trial variations in the number of attempts required to self-right showed that the animal's self-righting was stochastic (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The robot consisted of a head, two wings, a leg, and motors to actuate the wings and leg.
source: The robot consisted of a head, two wings, a leg, and motors to actuate the wings and leg (Figure 2B, Table 1).
evidence: Description of robot design shown in Figure 2B and Table 1

claim: Both robot wings opened by rolling and pitching about the body by the same angle to emulate the animal's wing opening.
source: To emulate the animal's wing opening, both robot wings opened by rolling and pitching about the body by the same angle (defined as wing opening amplitude, θwing; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Description of robot actuation shown in figures

claim: The robot used a pendulum leg which oscillated in the coronal plane by the same angle to both sides to simplify leg flailing of the animal.
source: To simplify leg flailing of the animal, the robot used a pendulum leg which oscillated in the coronal plane by the same angle to both sides (defined as leg oscillation amplitude, θleg; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: Description of robot actuation shown in figures

claim: The robot's wings were opened and closed repeatedly while oscillating its legs to generate repeated attempts observed in the animal.
source: We opened and closed the robot's wings (hereafter referred to as an attempt) repeatedly while oscillating its legs to generate repeated attempts observed in the animal.
evidence: Description of robot control strategy

claim: The animal was likely to move its leg before wings at the start of self-righting (59% of intact leg trials and 81% of modified leg trials).
source: Because the animal was likely to move its leg before wings at the start of self-righting (59% of intact leg trials and 81% of modified leg trials), for non-zero robot leg oscillation amplitudes, the first wing opening was started after completing one cycle of leg oscillation (0.4 s).
evidence: Observation from animal experiments

claim: For non-zero robot leg oscillation amplitudes, the first wing opening was started after completing one cycle of leg oscillation (0.4 s).
source: Because the animal was likely to move its leg before wings at the start of self-righting (59% of intact leg trials and 81% of modified leg trials), for non-zero robot leg oscillation amplitudes, the first wing opening was started after completing one cycle of leg oscillation (0.4 s).
evidence: Description of robot control strategy based on animal behavior

claim: The robot was tested by systematically varying leg oscillation amplitude (0°, 15°, 30°, 45°) and wing opening amplitude (60°, 72°, 83°).
source: We tested self-righting performance of the robot by systematically varying leg oscillation amplitude θleg (0°, 15°, 30°, 45°) and wing opening amplitude θwing (60°, 72°, 83°).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: Five trials were collected for each combination of wing opening and leg oscillation amplitude.
source: We collected five trials for each combination of θwing and θleg.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: A total of 60 trials with 134 attempts were collected for the robot experiments.
source: This resulted in a total of 60 trials with 134 attempts.
evidence: Description of sample size

claim: For geometrically similar objects, length should scale with mass and density as l ∝ (m/ρ)^(1/3).
source: For geometrically similar objects, length l should scale with mass m and density ρ as l ∝ (m/ρ)1/3 (Alexander, 2006).
evidence: Scaling relationship from Alexander, 2006

claim: For geometrically similar objects, potential energy should scale as E ∝ m^(4/3)ρ^(−1/3).
source: Following this, potential energy should scale as E ∝ m∙(m/ρ)1/3 ∝ m4/3ρ−1/3.
evidence: Derived scaling relationship based on gravitational potential energy

claim: The robot's length, thickness, and pitch potential energy barriers scaled up roughly as expected based on geometric similarity.
source: We found that the robot's length, thickness, and pitch potential energy barriers scaled up roughly as expected (Table 2).
evidence: Comparison result shown in Table 2

claim: The larger scaling factor for robot's width and roll potential energy barrier is due to the robot being designed wider to make self-righting via rolling more strenuous.
source: The larger scaling factor for robot's width and roll potential energy barrier is due to the robot being designed wider to make self-righting via rolling more strenuous.
evidence: Explanation of design choice

claim: The Froude numbers for the robot and both the intact and modified animals were similar (within a factor of 2).
source: We found that the Froude numbers for the robot and both the intact and modified animals were similar (within a factor of 2).
evidence: Comparison result described in the manuscript

claim: The dynamic similarity demonstrated that the robot provided a good physical model for studying the animal's self-righting.
source: This dynamic similarity demonstrated that the robot provided a good physical model for studying the animal's self-righting.
evidence: Conclusion based on dynamic similarity

claim: A level, flat, rigid wooden surface (60 cm × 60 cm) covered with sandpaper was used as the righting arena for robot experiments.
source: For robot experiments, we used a level, flat, rigid wooden surface (60 cm × 60 cm) covered with sandpaper as the righting arena.
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: Two synchronized webcams were used to record the robot experiment from top and side views at 30 frames s−1 and a resolution of 960 × 720 pixels.
source: We used two synchronized webcams (Logitech C920, Logitech, Newark, CA) to record the experiment from top and side views at 30 frames s−1 and a resolution of 960 × 720 pixels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: The robot body orientation relative to the lab coordinate system was recorded at approximately 56 Hz using the onboard IMU.
source: Using the onboard IMU, we recorded the robot body orientation relative to the lab coordinate system (X-Y-Z in Figure 2B) at ≈ 56 Hz and synchronized them with the motor actuation timings angles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom right).
evidence: Description of data collection

claim: The robot was actuated to repeatedly open and close its wings at 2 Hz and oscillate its legs at 2.5 Hz to self-right.
source: We then actuated the robot to repeatedly open and close its wings at 2 Hz and oscillate its legs at 2.5 Hz to self-right.
evidence: Description of robot actuation

claim: If the robot did not self-right after five wing opening attempts (10 s), it was powered down and reset for the next trial.
source: If the robot did not self-right after five wing opening attempts (10 s), we powered down the robot, stopped video recording, and reset the robot for the next trial.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol

claim: The robot was defined to have successfully self-righted if it attained an upright orientation within 10 s (five attempts).
source: We defined the robot to have successfully self-righted if it attained an upright orientation within 10 s (five attempts).
evidence: Definition of success criterion

claim: Among all the 134 attempts observed across all 60 trials, 44 attempts succeeded and 90 attempts failed.
source: Among all the 134 attempts observed across all 60 trials, 44 attempts succeeded (12, 15, and 17 attempts at θwing = 60°, 72°, and 83°, respectively), and 90 attempts failed (46, 27, and 17 attempts at θwing = 60°, 72°, and 83°, respectively).
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: The robot's 3D orientation in the lab frame was measured using Euler angles (yaw α, pitch β, and roll γ, Z-Y'-X' Tait-Bryan convention).
source: For each robot trial, we measured the robot's 3D orientation in the lab frame using Euler angles (yaw α, pitch β, and roll γ, Z-Y'-X' Tait-Bryan convention).
evidence: Description of measurement method

claim: The robot's center of mass was constrained to translate only along the vertical direction while maintaining contact with the ground.
source: Because the IMU measured only the 3D orientation of the robot, we constrained the robot's center of mass to translate only along the vertical direction (Figure 2B, Z-axis of lab frame) while maintaining contact with the ground (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Description of modeling constraint

claim: Pitch and roll kinetic energy were defined as the kinetic energy of the entire robot due to translational and rotational velocities along body fore-aft and lateral directions, respectively.
source: We defined pitch and roll kinetic energy as the kinetic energy of the entire robot due to translational and rotational velocities along body fore-aft and lateral directions, respectively.
evidence: Definition of kinetic energy components

claim: Vertical translation and yawing do not contribute to body pitching or rolling toward self-righting.
source: Because vertical translation and yawing do not contribute to body pitching or rolling toward self-righting, we did not consider vertical velocities or rotational velocities about the vertical axis.
evidence: Justification for modeling simplification

claim: The animal or robot did not lift off during self-righting, so in the model the lowest point was constrained to be always in contact with the ground.
source: Because the animal or robot did not lift off during self-righting, in the model we constrained the lowest point of the animal or robot to be always in contact with the ground.
evidence: Modeling constraint based on observation

claim: The potential energy depended on body pitch and roll, wing opening angle, and leg oscillation angle.
source: The potential energy depended on body pitch and roll, wing opening angle, and leg oscillation angle.
evidence: Description of model dependencies

claim: The effect of leg oscillation was modeled as a part of kinetic energy, so the leg was set to be held fixed in the middle when calculating the potential energy landscape.
source: Because the effect of leg oscillation was modeled as a part of kinetic energy, for simplicity, we set the leg to be held fixed in the middle when calculating the potential energy landscape.
evidence: Description of modeling simplification

claim: Potential energy landscape did not change considerably (roll barrier changed only up to 13%) when the leg moved.
source: We verified that potential energy landscape did not change considerably (roll barrier changed only up to 13%) when the leg moved.
evidence: Verification of modeling simplification

claim: Change in body yaw did not affect center of mass height because Euler angles were used for 3D rotations.
source: Because we used Euler angles for 3D rotations, change in body yaw did not affect center of mass height.
evidence: Property of Euler angle representation

claim: Wing opening angle was varied within the range [−10°, 90°] with a 0.5° increment in model calculations.
source: Because the robot's initial wing opening was negative (−6°) due to body weight, in our model calculations, we varied wing opening angle within the range [−10°, 90°] with a 0.5° increment.
evidence: Description of model parameter range

claim: For each wing opening angle, both body pitch and roll were varied within the range [−180°, 180°] with a 1° increment to calculate system potential energy.
source: For each wing opening angle, we then varied both body pitch and roll within the range [Note that for this range, the Euler angle description of body orientations has inherent redundancies. For example, body (pitch, roll) = (0°, −180°) and (pitch, roll) = (0°, 180°) describe the same physical orientation of the robot. However, this does not affect our modeling and conclusions, because the system state only reaches a redundant state toward the end of self-righting when it is near-upright.] [−180°, 180°] with a 1° increment and calculated zCoM to obtain the system potential energy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of model parameter range

claim: The pitch barrier was defined as the minimal barrier to escape from the metastable local minimum toward the pitch upright basin.
source: We defined the pitch and roll barriers as the minimal barriers to escape from the metastable local minimum toward the pitch and roll upright basins (Figure 5C, blue and red arrow).
evidence: Definition of pitch barrier shown in Figure 5C

claim: The roll barrier was defined as the minimal barrier to escape from the metastable local minimum toward the roll upright basins.
source: We defined the pitch and roll barriers as the minimal barriers to escape from the metastable local minimum toward the pitch and roll upright basins (Figure 5C, blue and red arrow).
evidence: Definition of roll barrier shown in Figure 5C

claim: The roll barrier was defined as the lowest potential energy barrier within ψ = ± [45°, 135°], because both roll upright minima always lay in this angular range.
source: We defined the roll barrier as the lowest potential energy barrier within ψ = ± [45°, 135°], because both roll upright minima always lay in this angular range.
evidence: Definition and justification of roll barrier

claim: The pitch barrier was defined as the potential energy barrier at ψ = 0° toward the pitch local minimum.
source: We defined the pitch barrier as the potential energy barrier at ψ = 0° toward the pitch local minimum.
evidence: Definition of pitch barrier

claim: Mixed-effects ANOVA was used to test whether the animal's percentage of time spent on winged and legged self-righting attempts and self-righting probability changed with leg modification.
source: We tested whether the animal's percentage of time spent on winged and legged self-righting attempts and self-righting probability changed with leg modification using a mixed-effects ANOVA, with leg treatment as the fixed factor and individual as a random factor to account for individual variability.
evidence: Description of statistical method

claim: ANOVA was used to test whether the animal's pitch and roll kinetic energy depended on leg modification.
source: We tested whether the animal's pitch and roll kinetic energy depended on leg modification using ANOVA with leg treatment a fixed factor.
evidence: Description of statistical method

claim: Chi-squared test was used to test whether the robot's self-righting probability depended on leg oscillation amplitude at each wing opening amplitude.
source: We tested whether the robot's self-righting probability, number of attempts required to self-right, pitch and roll kinetic energy depended on leg oscillation amplitude at each wing opening amplitude using a chi-squared test for probability and an ANOVA for the rest, with wing opening magnitude as a fixed factor.
evidence: Description of statistical method

claim: ANOVA was used to test whether the robot's number of attempts required to self-right, pitch and roll kinetic energy depended on leg oscillation amplitude at each wing opening amplitude.
source: We tested whether the robot's self-righting probability, number of attempts required to self-right, pitch and roll kinetic energy depended on leg oscillation amplitude at each wing opening amplitude using a chi-squared test for probability and an ANOVA for the rest, with wing opening magnitude as a fixed factor.
evidence: Description of statistical method

claim: All statistical tests were performed using JMP Pro 14.
source: All statistical tests were performed using JMP Pro 14 (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC).
evidence: Description of statistical software
